chain store = a shop that belongs to a group with many branches
outlet = a shop that sells last season's or factory goods cheaper
click and collect = ordering online and picking the goods up in a shop
convenience store = a small shop that sells everyday goods, often open late
boutique = a small shop that sells fashionable, often expensive clothes
charity shop = a shop that sells donated goods to raise money for a cause
DIY store = a large shop that sells tools, paint and building materials
flagship store = the main, largest shop of a brand, often in a capital city
shop-in-shop = a branded counter or small shop inside a larger store
independent retailer = a shop owner who is not part of a large chain
wholesaler = a business that sells goods in large amounts to shops
retail park = a group of large shops outside a town with a car park
pop-up shop = a shop that opens for a short time, then closes
off-licence = a shop that sells alcoholic drinks to take away
greengrocer's = a shop that sells fruit and vegetables
delicatessen = a shop that sells high-quality cheeses, meats and speciality food
hardware shop = a shop that sells tools, screws and household fittings
stationer's = a shop that sells pens, paper and office supplies
florist's = a shop that sells flowers and plants
launderette = a place with washing machines that the public can pay to use
pawnbroker's = a shop that lends money if you leave a valuable object as security
antique shop = a shop that sells old, valuable furniture or objects
shopping arcade = a covered passage with small shops on both sides
pedestrian precinct = a shopping area closed to cars
shop window = the glass front of a shop where goods are shown
fitting room = a small room in a clothes shop for trying clothes on
shop assistant = a person who helps customers and sells goods in a shop
shopkeeper = a person who owns or runs a small shop
cashier = the person who takes payment at a till
opening hours = the times when a shop or office is open to the public
browse = to look at goods in a shop without a plan to buy at once
shop around = to compare prices in different shops before you buy
in stock = available to buy now in the shop or warehouse
out of stock = not available to buy at the moment
sold out = with no items left to sell
window display = the arrangement of goods shown in a shop window
stockroom = the room where a shop keeps extra goods
self-checkout = a machine where you scan goods and pay without a cashier
till = the machine in a shop that records sales and holds money
barcode = the pattern of lines a scanner reads to identify a product
price tag = a small label showing how much something costs
loyalty card = a shop card that collects points or gives discounts
gift voucher = a ticket with a value that can be spent in a shop
carrier bag = a bag from a shop, often paper or plastic, for carrying goods
receipt = a piece of paper that proves you paid for goods
instalment = one of several payments for goods bought over time
interest rate = the extra percentage a bank charges or pays on money
overdraft = an arrangement to spend more money than is in your account
contactless = paying by tapping a card or phone without entering a PIN
counterfeit = made as a copy of something valuable in order to deceive
hire purchase = a system of paying in instalments and owning the goods at the end
pay a deposit = to pay a first sum to reserve goods or a service
advance payment = money paid before goods are delivered or work is finished
current account = a bank account for everyday spending and receiving pay
savings account = a bank account for money you do not spend at once
debit card = a card that takes money straight from your bank account
credit limit = the maximum amount you may spend on a credit card
interest-free = with no extra percentage charged if you pay on time
bank charges = fees a bank takes for services or for going into the red
direct debit = an instruction that lets a company take money from your account
standing order = an instruction to send a fixed sum from your account on set dates
bank transfer = sending money from one account to another electronically
chip and PIN = paying by putting a card in a machine and typing a secret number
digital wallet = an app that stores card details so you can pay with a phone
invoice = a document that lists goods or services and the money owed
VAT = a tax added to the price of many goods and services
proof of purchase = a receipt or document that shows you bought something
transaction = an act of buying, selling or moving money
bank statement = a list of money going in and out of your account
overdrawn = having spent more than is in your bank account
in the red = owing money to the bank; having a negative balance
in the black = having money left; not owing the bank
debt = money that you owe to a person or a bank
run up a debt = to gradually owe more and more money
pay off = to finish paying all the money you owe
exchange rate = how much one currency is worth in another
exchange commission = a fee charged for changing one currency into another
cashpoint = a machine in a wall that gives you cash from your account
building society = a financial organisation that offers savings accounts and mortgages
lump sum = an amount of money paid all at once, not in parts
surcharge = an extra amount added to a price for a particular reason
handling fee = a small extra charge for processing an order or payment
postage and packing = the extra you pay for wrapping and sending goods
cashback = money returned as a reward, or extra cash taken at a shop till
online banking = managing your bank account through a website
mobile banking = managing your bank account on a smartphone app
credit rating = a judgement of how likely you are to repay borrowed money
card fraud = crime that uses stolen card details to buy goods or take money
withdraw cash = to take money out of a bank account as notes
bank balance = the amount of money in an account at a given time
overspend = to spend more money than you planned or can afford
keep to a budget = to spend only the amount of money you have planned
disposable income = money left after tax and essential bills, for spending or saving
go bust = to fail financially and close a business (informal)
creditworthy = judged likely to repay a loan on time
haggle = to argue about the price in order to pay less
extortionate = far too expensive; unreasonably high in price
guarantee = a promise to repair or replace goods if they fail within a period
live on a shoestring = to live on very little money
tighten one's belt = to spend less because money is short
endorsement = public support for a product, often by a well-known person
target audience = the group of people an advert is designed to reach
misleading advert = an advertisement that gives a false or unclear impression
commercial = an advertisement on television or radio
billboard = a large outdoor board used to advertise a product
flyer = a small sheet of paper advertising an event or product
slogan = a short, memorable phrase used in advertising
jingle = a short, catchy tune used in a radio or TV advert
brand awareness = how well people recognise and remember a brand
product placement = showing a branded product in a film or programme as advertising
celebrity endorsement = when a famous person is paid to recommend a product
junk mail = unwanted advertising letters sent to your home
pop-up advert = an advert that appears suddenly on a website or app
classified ad = a short advertisement in a newspaper or website, often for jobs or goods
mailshot = a large number of advertising letters sent at the same time
cold calling = phoning people you do not know in order to sell something
hard sell = an aggressive way of trying to make someone buy at once
selling point = a feature that makes people want to buy one product rather than another
word of mouth = people recommending a product by talking about it
viral marketing = advertising designed to be shared quickly online
sponsored post = a social-media message that a company has paid to promote
banner ad = a rectangular advert across a website
catalogue = a booklet or site listing goods you can order
leaflet = a folded sheet of paper with information or advertising
advertising campaign = a planned series of adverts for one product or cause
brand image = the idea people have of a company and its products
small print = the detailed conditions, often in tiny letters, at the bottom of a contract
free sample = a small amount of a product given away so you can try it
promotional offer = a special deal used to attract customers for a limited time
customer = a person who buys goods or services from a shop or company
refund = money you get back when you return goods or cancel a service
warranty = a written promise that a product will work for a stated period
faulty = not working correctly because of a defect
ombudsman = an official who investigates complaints against companies or services
after-sales service = help, repairs and advice after you have bought a product
return policy = the shop's rules about bringing goods back
money-back guarantee = a promise that you will get your money back if you are not satisfied
replacement = a new item given instead of one that is faulty or unsuitable
compensation = money paid because goods or a service caused loss or harm
cooling-off period = a set time after a sale when you may cancel without a penalty
consumer rights = the legal protections a buyer has when purchasing goods or services
consumer protection = laws and bodies that stop shops and advertisers treating buyers unfairly
small claims court = a court that deals with modest money disputes without a full trial
Trading Standards = the official service that checks shops follow consumer law
not fit for purpose = unsuitable for the use the seller said it was for
as described = matching the details the seller gave before you bought it
ordinary wear = the normal damage that happens when something is used as intended
product recall = when a company asks customers to return a dangerous or faulty product
malfunction = to stop working correctly
damaged goods = items that are broken, stained or spoiled when they arrive
late delivery = goods arriving after the date that was promised
tracking number = a code that lets you follow a parcel on its journey
dispatch = to send goods from a warehouse to a customer
make a complaint = to formally say that you are not satisfied with goods or a service
extended warranty = extra cover, often paid for, after the free guarantee ends
plumber = a person whose job is to fit and repair water pipes and toilets
electrician = a person whose job is to fit and repair electrical systems
locksmith = a person who fits, opens and repairs locks
mechanic = a person who repairs engines and vehicles
dry-cleaner's = a shop that cleans clothes you cannot wash at home
beautician = a person who gives beauty treatments such as facials and nails
call-out charge = a fee for a worker to come to your home, before any repair
hourly rate = the amount a worker charges for each hour of work
quote = a written price offered for a job before the work begins
gratuity = money given to staff for good service, sometimes added to a bill
tradesperson = a skilled worker such as a plumber, electrician or carpenter
boycott = refusing to buy from a company as a protest
impulse buy = something you buy suddenly without planning
planned obsolescence = designing goods to wear out or go out of date so people buy again
ethical shopping = choosing goods made without harm to people, animals or the planet
ethically sourced = obtained in a way that treats workers and producers fairly
sweatshop = a factory with very poor pay and conditions
shopaholic = a person who cannot stop buying things, even if they do not need them
retail therapy = buying things in order to cheer yourself up
designer label = clothes or goods with a famous fashion designer's name
own-brand = a product sold under the supermarket's own name, usually cheaper
upmarket = intended for richer customers; high quality and expensive
mass-produced = made in large numbers by machines, not by hand
throwaway society = a culture that throws things away instead of repairing them
consumerism = the idea that buying more and more goods is a good way to live
